I kind of got used to the design, but still they could have colored buttons well. this is good for music listening, but for talking on phone i would doubt the ease of use.4) display is great and crisp.I have seen too many reviews about the unit dying after a month of usage. I will report back after 1 month of using this. I use this about 5-6 hours a day at my work.
LOVE LOVE LOVE these headphones. They have amazing sound quality. I use them for a bluetooth headset, radio, and music headphones. A must buy.

Product was exactly as described and arrived in original, unopened packaging.My only complaint is the placement of the Left/Right splitting of the earbud cables.  The left side is too short and the right too long.  It makes it awkward and sloppy.

Just received this and first impression is a good one.  I bought this to use primarily as wireless headset for my iPod Touch and it works well and the FM radio is a nice bonus.  As someone else mentioned, the only real issue I have is the volume adjustment is very sensitive and easily moved up or down inadvertently. A volume/control lock would have made this item a real winner and a five star rating.
summary: Innovative device with one minor glitch!

reviewText: Versatile in use and convenient. I can plug in my own choice of headphones/earphones as per the occasion. So it could be my sport earphones while in Gym, Aux-in for car, both for listening to podcasts/musics and phone calls (This itself is worth the money!)Couple of gripes: 1. the grip is.. let's say pretty useless. 2. sweat can damage the device, in fact majority of the complaints are from damage due to sweat.Keep it away from necks and arms while exercising (I keep it inside my pocket). Yes, there are cables involved but at least they're connected to this itsy-bitsy device not a humongous phone!

There was a lot to like about this headset.  I bought it primarily for use at the gym.  The best feature of this headset is that it's got a great clip that expands easily.  I used this for music at the gym with an iPhone 4.  Pairing was not a problem.  Charging was initially not a problem.  The music quality was spot on and not a problem.  I will confess that I didn't use their ear buds but went with a pair of Sennheiser earbuds that wrap onto my ears.  (no slippage during a run)My troubles started with intermittent failures to charge.  First the unit wouldn't turn on.  So I'd charge it again.  The next time, it would appear to charge but not hold a charge.  Then finally, it wouldn't turn on at all.  I do not believe that it was sweat related as it was clipped to the back of my shirt, facing away from my body.  I did attempt to be delicate around this unit with my gym gear.  Either I lost track of the units delicacy or it died.  I'm not sure which.  Regardless, I can't recommend it since mine died.  Maybe if I tried again... It seems like all too often units designed for gym usage/outdoors live only for a short while before giving up.  Case in point here.
summary: I liked this until it died.

reviewText: The clip is not strong enough.  And there is no lock out function so I am constantly voice dialing my iPhone and pausing the music and stuff.  It is just an awkward design. I switched over to Lg Tone (Hbs-700) for the gym and am much happier.

This device is almost perfect, from my perspective. I wanted something that has FM Tuner and bluetooth so I can listen to EITHER the radio (I am an NPR junkie) or my music in stereo (I have a Palm Pre Plus). Also, I could use my own headphones (priceySony MDREX36V/BLK EX Earbud Headphone (Black)). The unit paired up nicely with my smartphone, as well as my bluetooth-enabled netbook. So far so good.The volume control is garbage, as other reviewers have mentioned, but I could live with that little gripe. I also wish the unit allowed for radio presets, because I often toggle between 2 different NPR stations... but in the grands scheme that's minor.Alas, all this was too good to be true. After a few weeks of use, the first one suddenly refused to turn on (if memory serves me, this was right after a grueling workout session). I even tried in vain to recharge it. Fortunately it was still within the return period, so I took advantage of Amazon.com's no-hassle return/exchange policy and got a new unit sent to me.After a few weeks, I clearly remember one day when I was sweating especially heavily at the gym, and the unit got a bit tangled up on my shirt (like many people mentioned, it doesn't clip well). I am pretty sure sweat got into it. Poof. Stopped working. Would not turn on. Came back home, plugged it in... the "charging" indicator lit up, but even after hours, the unit would never turn back on.And then I found I'd missed the Return/Exchange window by a few days.Extreme SadFace.So I concluded: It must have been sweat damage that took out the first one as well.So this is the THIRD unit I am getting, and this time I am paying money again. That's how much I like this device. I'll be sure to be very careful with it at the gym, and maybe buy/create a little plastic bag for it for protection.But if this 3rd one fails, I'll have to give up and try a different solution that integrates with my lifestyle like thisSony Ericsson Hi-Fi Bluetooth Stereo Headset with FM Radiodid.Wish me luck... will post update whenever I can.

I am currently using this with my Samsung Galaxy Nexus, where the sound quality is great, the controls work, and the range is good (I can get about 30 feet in an open room with no problems). I mostly use this while listening to music at my desk at work, where I'm moving around a lot and don't want to have cords in my way. The Nexus does not seem to work with the display on the Sony though -- song titles aren't shown. It did work properly with my iPad when I tried it.Battery life is pretty good. I've listened to music for 3 hours and had plenty of battery left; I have yet to run it completely down.My only real gripe is the touch sensitive volume controls -- I inadvertently change the volume every time I touch the device it seems.As for call quality, I have an easier time hearing people I'm calling with this compared to my previous headset, a Blueant Q1. I don't think that people I was calling heard much of a difference though.Overall, I'd recommend this if you are looking for a stereo Bluetooth receiver that works with any pair of headphones. I just wish Google would hurry up and update their Bluetooth stack so I can use the display on this thing!

FM radio almost useless as it hisses a lot and therefore not useful.Not a good range.Connecting and reconnecting to different devices is a hassle.I replaced it with the Jabra clip and have been impressed withit so far though the this one's range is better.

I had purchased this for my car stereo so I could hook up my Galaxy Nexus to the stereo without wires. But I wanted something that could control changing tracks. Now this product was great with my galaxy nexus but not without its quirks.Pros:Very loud volume from my Android devicePlay/Pause ff/rw all worked without issueAble to pair multiple devices (but switching took some attention)On screen display very informativeDecent battery life, I would get about 4-8 hours of playDecent headphonesCons:The volume rocker is touch based and sometimes took a bit to change the volumeSwitching between BT devices was a bit confusing at first and required some researchHad to force repair with my phone after about a week of use, it would connect but would not pickup any audio.Overall, I rate the device high, Higher than I would the Samsung options, I have owned multiple Samsung bluetooth devices like this one and non were as "loud" or clear as the Sony.
summary: Works but not without its quirks

reviewText: They're alright for talking on the phone but as usual people complain on the other end of the call that the back round noise is to loud. Great for listing to music!

Good compatibility: I've used it on Samsung Nexus 4g and Samsung Galaxy S II Android phones, one PC with build-in bluetooth chip and one PC with USB-bluetooth adapter (bluetooth 4.0). The MW600 headset works flawlessly with those equipments. Very easy to pair and connect.Great sound quality: No noise or interference at all even in a room with more than 10 WIFI access point signals, wireless mouse, and wireless phone. The sound is crystal clear at least for a non-professional music fan.Flexibility: You can change the earphone by yourself if you don't like the one coming within the package. Any 3.5mm jack earphone will work.Great battery life: Standby time is super long that you don't have to turn it off when you don't need it. Probably weeks. Regarding to the streaming, I heavily use it for 3-4 hours a day and only need to recharge it every 3-4 days.Fast charging: The charging time is short and around 2-3 hours. It has a standard micro USB port, so actually you don't really need the SONY changer. Any micro USB charger that works with your Android/Blackberry/WP7 smartphone will work on this headset.

The good news is that the sound (using your own headphones of course) and battery life are good. But it immediately became clear that design of the thing is pretty dumb. There is a digital display that is useless because the thing is clipped to your shirt so you can never read it anyway.  Because of the shape, when clipped to something like a t-shirt, it leans forward, flipping over the shirt. You also end up bumping your chin on it when you look down unless you angle it a lot. The volume control is terrible (points trying to be creative though). Its very easy to accidentally change the volume when trying to operate the buttons on the other side you need to squeeze the device. It also sometimes doesnt work at times when you do want to change the volume.All of these issues could have been easily fixed if they just made it as close to an iPod Shuffle as possible w/o getting sued. If it were the square shape, you wouldnt have the issue if it leaning forward. If the buttons were like that you would have to worry about accidentally hitting volume.All that said, its still perfectly usable. I might stick with it because there is no decent alternative that lets you use your own headphones. Hopefully someone will improve upon this soon. Wouldn't be hard.Pros:You can use your own headphonesCons:Stick shape not ideal (see above)Volume control has issues (see above)If you have headphones that have a remote on them, they won't work anymore (prob a bluetooth thing). You have to use the controls on this unit.
summary: Wrong shape, should be like a Shuffle

reviewText: I was going to give this five stars until I tried to connect it to my Windows 7 laptop. (Details below)Pros:- Small- Light weight- Phone calls sound good- Stereo sound quality is great- Nice comfy ear buds (and seem to almost totally seal out the rest of the world.)- Battery life is good- Nice clip to attach to clothing- Pairing was easy (for the phone)- Pairing was easy (for a Mac)- FM radio (although I don't use it)Cons:- Not real crazy about the {one-shorter-than-the-other} cord on the headset, and the left one is a bit too short for my tastes. But with the longer cord draped around the back of my neck, it's functional and not a deal breaker.- Uhm... Doesn't work with Windows 7?  O_oSo, here we go...The sound quality on this thing is great. I actually loved the headphones that come with it, and I am using them separately for other purposes. They fit snugly in the ear, and almost completely seal out any outside noise. When using the phone, others are telling me it sounds good on their end also.Very easy to use and set up.So, it was turning out to be a perfect device. Except...Well, I was going to throw up all five stars on this device until I actually bought one for myself. I had previously bought one of these for my girlfriend. It was perfect. It connected effortlessly to her Android phone, and then just as easy to her Mac. She was totally happy running around the house listening with the music transmitting from her laptop. She was happy, I was happy. And now I wanted one.So I bought one for myself. It connected perfect to my Android phone. Then I went to connect it to MY Sony Vaio, Windows 7 Pro, (64 bit) laptop.(Here's where it actually gets funny.)Apparently Sony doesn't have drivers for Windows 7, for this device, NOR does Microsoft, and Sony states that it doesn't work with Windows 7 (Uhm... hello? it's only currently THE most used operating system in the world.).So neither Sony nor Microsoft appear to be caring at all. (As if this is some kind of a stand-off, and both are being stubborn about who should develop drivers for this thing.)So I go to Sony's web site, only to be informed that I had to go to Sony Ericsson's web site. (Okay, Sony is NOT Sony Ericsson, "whatever") But there wasn't anything there either.And what's even more ironic is that my laptop is a Sony Vaio. So my new little Sony device won't connect to my Sony computer. (Nice)However, I did some searching around the web and found a weird solution, and it actually works with Windows 7 now.I downloaded and installed this program from Lenovo:[...]And now, since today is my birthday, I am reasonably happy  :)
summary: Great device!  AND I got it to work with Windows 7!

reviewText: This is a great headset ! Sounds good , battery last all day with radio . Connected to phone easy , calls are ok, wife said it was clear but sounded like I was in a tunnel. I would have given it 5 stars but ..... The clip is flimsy and will not hold it in my pocket. I lost it after the second day.Good thing I bought 2.

Just received this nifty little device.  It is very small, light, well built (not waterproof), and easy to use.  It comes partially electrically charged out of the box.  Following instructions, it paired to my iPhone 4 and iPad immediately without problems or the need to enter any security codes on the Apple devices.  I can now use either Apple device with a simple setting change on the MW600. What a great little unit.  I'm now walking around my house listening to music from my iPad.The unit comes with detachable noise isolating earphones.  The cord to the left ear is much shorter than the cord to the right ear.  Sound is on par with good under $30 earphones, which is to say quite adequate.  Bluetooth sound quality is very good.  I hear no background noise, whistling, interference or other artifacts.  Voice and music sound are solid and are very listenable, almost as good as through wired earphones to my iPhone and iPad.The MW600 also has an FM radio which picks up all my local stations.  Unfortunately it does not have FM station preset memories.  You must manually tune or scan for the next station.  This feature would be most welcome as I have ten very good FM stations in my local area.  FM sound quality is good.Using it with my iPad playing music, I'm moving around my house, up to 30 feet away, into other rooms.  The device receives a signal at this 30 foot distance in other rooms through drywall.  Beyond this distance it cuts out.  I haven't attempted use outside of my house but it would problably be slightly more than 30 feet.  Reception distance is perfectly adequate and about the same as my other Bluetooth devices.Tried it with my iPhone calling my home phone answering machine.  The mic works fine, without any background noise.  The unit stops other functions while it makes or receives a call.  Once the call is complete, the previous mode, such as music listening comes gradually back up to its previous volume.  Nice feature.The receiver is a little tube, 2.5 inches long and ballpoint pen diameter, with a clip which attaches to my collar or inside shirt pocket.  The phone mic is on the end of the tube.  The little OLED display is easy to read and quite handy for changing and checking settings, including battery status.  It turns itself off after a few seconds to conserve power.  The earphone cords are different lengths as I've mentioned.  The left side is about seven inches long and the right side over a foot.  I like this as I can put the device in my shirt pocket, connect up the earplugs and not have alot of excess cord.  This arrangement doesn't allow the device to go into a pant pocket or be clipped to a belt.  For that, I'd need my other earphones with longer cords.  This is a great advantage with this unit.  I can use a variety of earphone/headphones.Also included is a small wall charger with mini-USB plug on the end.  I also received two additional sets of rubber earplug covers to accomodate different sized ear openings.  The instruction sheet is thorough and complete.I'm really happy with this great little bluetooth device.  It replaces Motorola S305 headphones which never really fit right and always felt strange when wearing eyeglasses.
summary: Pairs to iPhone 4 and iPad Perfectly

reviewText: This was apparently a euro device because it shipped with a euro plug in ac adapter and an adapter from that to a US plug.  Not optical but I'll deal with it.
summary: The Sony MW600 works great...love it.

reviewText: The great thing about the Sony Bluetooth Headset is it makes headphones with a mini plug easier to manage. It frees up your bluetooth product (i.e. iPhone, iPad, computer) so you can move around freely. The reason I gave it 4 stars out of five, is because I constantly have to Re-Pair with my bluetooth items. Not always easy.

I upgraded to these headphones from another set in order to get better battery life, but I was not expecting the phenomenal range improvement. More than once now I have "lost" my phone while still listening to music on it, because I can wander throughout my 2500 sft two story house without losing connectivity. The multi device connectivity is interesting... took some getting used to selecting between three devices on the phones, but now I like it.

I couldn't decide which product was better nor could I find anyone that had compared each of these side by side, so I am attempting to do so now:Setup:Upon purchasing and receiving the two Bluetooth Headset Adapters, I unboxed and charged them fully before testing. I utilized the headsets that came with the units along with a control set of Ultimate Ears TripleFi 10 vi In Ear Monitors. I tested everything with my Apple iPhone 4s (Sprint) using iOS 5.0.1 and my Late 2011 MacBook Pro 15" using OS 10.7.3 (Lion) for the tests. Music comparisons used were Creed - Full Circle, Les Miserables - The Complete Symphonic Recording, Beethoven -The Immortal Collection and Nightwish - Angels Fall First. I also utilized World of Warcraft for gaming on my laptop with these headsets as well playing for at least an hour while questing.Unboxing:It goes without saying (but I'll say it here anyway), that most of these devices have a generic look and feel to them. I mean how much can you do with a Bluetooth Headset adapter? Even so, the packaging was actually very well done on both items. No plastic to cut, no annoying twist ties to get anything out of the box. Just the closed box and tape holding the flap closed. Both the Sony and the Samsung had nice presentation of the device and both were very easy to remove and start using. Both of these devices utilize MicroUSB chargers, so if you have other devices that use those connections, you only need to carry one type of charger to charge all of them.Initial Thoughts:After the unboxing and initial charging of both items, I decided to take a closer look at each item. Here are the lists of my thoughts on each item upon first inspection:Sony: I really like the display on this device. Very bright when needed and then shuts off. No annoying flashing lights or any other attention getting gimmicks. The buttons are nice to the touch and the Play/Pause button is slightly raised to make it easy to hit it. I dislike the push and hold power on button as I prefer the sliding switch, but it wasn't like Sony used the button for anything else, so not a problem. The clip on the MW600 seems a bit weak and seems a bit on the flimsy side, so that might be a problem. BTW, this device has a radio and it does support RDS so it shows the song title, station ID, etc, but this feature is useless for me as I can't stand to listen to commercials so, I don't use the radio. The size of the this device is very nice, but for clipping on my work shirts, this item is a bit thicker than I'd like. The charging port on this device is open... I am not sure that I care to have the connectors open all of the time on this device while wearing this potentially everywhere. I am sure this was done to avoid using dust covers, but I think this would have been a good idea.Samsung: I like the feel of this device in the hands... It feels sturdy without being heavy or bulky. I dislike the single blue/purple/red LED on the front of the device to indicate battery, use, etc as I dislike attention getting flashing lights, but LED is useful as it does indicate the battery level. I really like the power switch on this device. It the perfect tension as to not turn on when you don't want it to and not too stiff as to require too much force to turn it on. I have the Bose Bluetooth headset that I often turn on by accident when putting away, so this switch is a nice change from that headset. Also the Play/Pause button is indented slightly from the other buttons making it easy to find as well. Personally, I think I like the button better on the Sony as my fingers naturally find the extended button easier than the indented one... But I supposed engineers for Samsung were worried someone might accidentally press it if anything stuck out. Only time will tell on that. This device is the larger of the two being roughly twice the width of the Sony device, but it's half as thick. I think this will be better for my work shirts as I can hide most of this device in the shirt. The clip is very nicely done on this device and the charging port has a dust cover.Initial Usage:After turning the devices on and pairing with my phone and computer, here are my thoughts on their usage before I take them out with me on the road. BTW, pairing on each of these devices was very simple and I never had to enter a code anywhere for the devices to work. Incidentally, if you decide to use these devices the pin code for both is 0000 if required by your phone or computer. Oh and both devices worked with Siri on the iPhone. I was pleasantly surprised how well both functioned. Also, both headset adapters came with headphones that have a short cable... This is very nice because it allows for the wearer to have the clip where it can be reached without 4 foot of extra cable hanging about.Sony: I have to say that the display is the nicest feature of this device. It shows when you need pairing and when the device is connected. It shows the time on the display once connected to my phone and while playing the track is displayed as well. When using the next or previous buttons, it also shows what's happening as well. Also, the battery indicator is always present on the display as the battery graph most phones have today. After playing with the basic functions of the headset, I found that everything was very well done except the volume buttons. I guess you really can't call them buttons and it's not really a slide either. The surface is flat and has very slight marking indicating + and - and you slide your finger in the direction of either to turn it up or down. Two things about this make this a really by design. 1) You can't figure out which is which by feel. Without looking at the device it is hard to figure out how to turn up or down the volume. 2) It is very easy to change the volume accidentally while handing the device. Since this design doesn't work with an indentation or some other means of force, while holding the device to look at the time you can easily change the volume of your music/call/radio. This device supports multiple devices so when pairing with a computer and a phone you don't have to pair each time you use it. Not sure how useful this item really is, but could be nice for those that use more than one device to connect to their headphones. Volume changes on the headset does change the volume on the phone. This is nice for the fact that you can change the volume from either the phone or the headset and the volume indicators are the same.Samsung: The coolest feature of this device is the voice prompts. Immediately on startup you have a Voice Prompt of Power On. Further, it goes into pairing mode and gives you the code while waiting for you to connect. A nice feature as you don't have to look up anything. When you flip the switch, it gives you a voice prompt of Power Off... It seems a bit basic, but it is actually nice when you have the confirmation without having to look at the device to tell if it's on or off. (BTW, you can turn off the Voice Prompts.) The button layout seems to be setup nicely for operating everything by touch. All buttons are slightly different places or offset in comparison to other buttons, so it makes it easy to determine which side of the device and which button you are actually going to depress. My biggest disappointment here is Sound Alive feature. While some people may like their bluetooth devices to control EQ, I do not. If I want to adjust the EQ, I want my Music Player to do it... So this feature means that when you press the button, the audio changed to add or remove Bass. While I can see this being useful on Phone calls, this button works all of the time, so I have to be careful to not turn on the feature. This is one of those items I would prefer a press and hold to enable it. The feature I like best on this phone is the volume control. Unlike the Sony, I can change the volume on the phone and the headset adapter independently. This gives me a very nice granular control of how loud or soft I can make the volume. When using the IEMs (In Ear Monitors) this feature is very nice. I can turn down the volume enough to sleep with at home or turn it up enough to work at noisy environments equally. I can see how some people wouldn't like this, but since my IEMs have 26 DB of sound attenuation, I have a very quiet noise floor to start from and I can thereby keep my music volume very low while maintaining a good volume in ear. This keeps my hearing in tact while allowing for a very enjoyable listening experience.Audio Quality:Let me start on this section with a bit of theory and human nature. First, I am an audio engineer for a medium sized church and I do live sound mixing 8 hours a week. Further, I have to train others to run the mixer for live sound often enough that I know a thing or two about how people perceive sound. Since most people don't listen for hours on end to the details that comprise music (IE how well the drum mix works with the vocal mix, etc) and since most people can't hear the difference between the 128Kbps and the 256Kbps MP3s they get from Amazon or elsewhere, I am not going into an expanded discussion on how good or bad these are. I am not saying that people won't notice that something is different, I am saying they won't know what is different or how the difference effects their music experience. Since all of the audio sources I used are from 256Kbps encoded sources, I am sure that the limit of the technology of the music source is the biggest limiting factor in the audio quality and therefore all comparisons are extremely subjective unless I were to grab lossless files and spend hours listening to the same songs over and over in order to give a details analysis of how good the Bluetooth transmits those high bandwidth songs. Long story short, please forgive me for not going into detail about the entirety of the audio quality and using generalizations instead.Sony: The audio quality of these adapters were quite adequate and I couldn't hear any significant loss of fidelity using my IEMs with this device and plugging into the iPhone. I will say that the Sony headphones provided with the device were a pleasant surprise. Normally Sony likes to drive their Bass much more than everything else as most people like to bring the Bass out when listening to their music. These headphones were actually quite flat and for single drivers were very decent for daily use. I did also try these while sleeping and they fit nicely in the ear to allow for you to put them in on the plane and take a nap. Also, the headphones were comfortable and didn't hurt after long use. The headphones do isolate but not nearly as much as my IEMs. However, for daily use at work or about town, that's probably a good thing. The only thing about these headphones I disliked was that the short part of the cord was on my left while the device when clipped to my shirt faced the cable to the right... This made for some tugging on the left, while not having any problems on the right. Also, the audio quality of the phone calls made with this device was as good as any wired headphones I have tried. Overall, the audio quality on these were quite sufficient for daily use, but if you are the serious audiophile, you are probably listening with High Quality Monitors and Lossless Music and these aren't for you.Samsung: The audio with this adapter and my IEMs were amazing considering the technology behind streaming music wirelessly. I think that stems from how the bluetooth on these function and the profiles it supports. Since these are newer, one would expect some improvement over other models that are much older and these don't disappoint. The headphones that come with these are pretty much worthless. They don't provide much in the way of isolation and they are so obviously single drivers. I am not sure how much people would buy either of these devices because of the headphones packaged with the devices, but with a build quality like this from Samsung, they are better off dropping the headphones in the package and bringing the price of this device down some more. It would certainly probably help with the reviews from people complaining about audio quality. Call Audio was also decent. Again, I would say that daily use of this device would be very adequate. If pressed to give a nod to either of these devices on audio alone, I would choose the Samsung providing that you don't use the included headphones.The Work Test:This is what my planned use for these devices is and this is really where I need to see how these function. I didn't do as much prep on this as I did with everything else, so this section is mainly my preferences and my expectations of the device.Sony: My initial problems with the volume didn't turn out to be a problem while working. I only had to adjust the volume once as most of the time, I just removed the headphones when needed. Also, my initial praise for the display turns out to be misguided as well. I never once went to the headset display to do anything. Since I needed to press a button on the phone to accept forwarded calls from work, I just picked up the phone each time thereby making the display unimportant. Also, the clip did turn out to be a problem, but only because of the Sony headphones. If I were using something else, I think the clip would be ok, but as it was, the left ear headphone will pull the device from my shirt. I finally swapped the headphones from left and right and solved my problem. Also, since I synced these with my computer, I had to go through the interface to change everything back to phone from computer just to see the time and have Siri working again. Not a huge deal, but it keeps it from being useful that I can connect this device to multiple sources.Samsung: Overall, these worked best for how I do my daily work and allowed for me to use Siri, answer the phone and listed to music without getting my headset tangled in coats, desks, etc.Overall, I give the edge to Samsung as they are 33% less than the Sony's, have slightly a better sound and work better for what I need than the Sony's. Honestly though, either device is actually very good considering the cost and either should work for anyone that is looking to get their cables out of the way while still using cabled headphones. I give them both 4 stars (Amazon represents this as I Like It and I do.)

I understand the challenge that Sony faced when designing this headset: a small surface area with a lot of button options. I've never owned a different pair of bluetooth headphones. So maybe they're all screwed up like this one. But the button configuration on this thing can be maddening. if you just want to unclip it and move it, be careful or you'll activate the "next track" button or the pause button. Try to grab it differently and you activate the voice control button. And the volume control is a touch sensive slider that isn't very touch sensitive.Also, the way the cord is designed, there's no good place to attach the control fob where the cord isn't poking you in the face or pulling out your earbuds.On the plus side, the earbuds are tight fitting and block a lot of noise even with the music off. The sound quality is adequate for me as I mostly use these while on the lawnmower or tractor.Overall, though, I would pass on these in favor of something a little more ergonomic.

I've been using an old iPod shuffle while working out at the gym.  I've been waiting to switch to using my Android phone instead but didn't want to hold me phone or use a bulky armband.  I had seen too many people drop or yank their phones off the console.  I came across this device and ordered it figuring it could solve my problem and it did, perfectly. With the WM-600 I can leave my phone on the treadmill or elliptical console and not worry about dropping it or yanking it off.  It also allows me to take and make calls and works flawlessly with my phone (Motorola Atrix).
summary: Perfect solution to working out at the gym with my phone

reviewText: I really wanted this to work.  I've been searching for the perfect solution to my cell phone use for a long time and I thought this might be it.  My needs are for a dual ear Bluetooth headset (due to age related hearing loss combined with working in a noisy environment) combined with a noise canceling microphone (again due to the noisy environment).  I do a lot of business on my cell phone- I'm in business banking and am on the go a lot, so I need to do business in rental cars, at airports, in restaurants etc.  But I am getting on in years, so for me to be able to hear, it's a lot better if the sound is coming in through both ears and the headset also blocks out external noise.  I've tried over 10 different Bluetooth devices over the past 7 years, and this seemed to be the answer.  Sleek form factor.  Dual earbuds.  And Sony quality.  Or so I hoped.First the good: if you want these primarily for listening to music, with only an occasional phone conversation, then this is a 5 star product.  Music played through this (from a Droid RAZR as well as an LG Octane) was absolutely first rate.  I owned a hifi store for 22 years, and while my high frequency hearing isn't what it used to be, I can still hear coloration and distortion, and of all the Bluetooth headsets I've tried, this was by far the best.  In fact it compares favorably to mid-priced wired earbuds, and is much better that the iCrap buds that come with Apple devices.  And for speech, they are amazing.  I heard phone conversations better than with any other phone/headset device I've ever used.But here's the bad- my callers said my voice was muffled, distorted, and that they could hear EVERYTHING going on around me.  I had hoped that since I could clip this to the collar on my shirt, barely 2" from my mouth, that my voice would be clear compared to other devices where the mic is next to my ear, but no such luck.  That, unfortunately, is a deal breaker for me.Battery life was fine, I love that you can use different earbuds with this (although the ones that come with it are excellent) so if the cable develops an intermittent you don't have to chuck the whole thing.  The different length cords allow you to run the left earbud cord behind your neck and out of the way.  And the price is most certainly right.  So as I said, if you mostly want to listen to music without the tether of a cord, you've come to the right place.  But for phone conversations, it just doesn't cut it.
summary: For listening, 5 stars- for talking, not so much

reviewText: EDIT: 1-19-13 Now that I have a new device to work with this, I have not had as many disconnect problems as listed below. reviewText: If you are looking to have wireless connection to your Zumo 660 GPS for music while riding a motorcycle, this item comes in handy.This is my second test of this device.  I returned the first one because, at that time, I was testing a Zumo 550 which has Bluetooth capability, but the 550 uses older Bluetooth protocols (prior to A2DP) so it only had low-grade mono Bluetooth.  This was fine for linking in your cell phone or getting spoken instructions, but it was lousy for music reproduction.  The sound quality stunk on ice, but I then held that the 550 was to blame.  As a result, I put the 550 up for sale and returned this BT receiver until I could obtain a Zumo 660 which uses A2DP protocol.I knew when I got the 660 this would be my first choice for testing the quality of Bluetooth reception, and I was not disappointed.  I plugged in a set of good quality headphones (as earbuds tend to sound "tinny"), and the MP3 playback from the Zumo 660 was as clear as if I was listening off my normal MP3 player.The only "con" I note with the Sony Ericsson is that when paired with a Garmin Zumo 660 the "play/pause", "skip forward" and "skip back" buttons on do not interact with the Garmin Zumo 660.  As I understand Bluetooth, this is a pairing issue that can vary from device to device.  I know the Sony works as designed because this shortcoming did not happen when it was paired with my iPhone.  This IS NOT a deal-breaker for me as I intend to manipulate the player via the controls on the GPS and not on the Sony as the receiver will always be tucked inside my jacket where I can't reach it while riding.  I can't say for certain what the full range of the receiver is, but I left the Zumo 660 at one end of the house and walked to the other end with no degradation in sound quality.  So, that's at least 50 feet or so...more than I'll ever need.So, if you have a Garmin Zumo 660 or 665 and don't mind that the controls on the device WILL NOT interface back to the GPS but want a quality BT receiver for listening to tunes, GPS and phone, this is a great deal.
summary: Works well with Garmin Zumo 660 GPS

I had several bluetooth stereo headsets and one bluetooth headphone adapter before so I have a bit of experience with these.After a couple of weeks I have found this to be quite excellent.  One of my complaints about other bluetooth devices was how long they took to power on and off.  This device does both of those actions quickly.  Although the power button is rather small and you have to pretty much look at the device to find it.This also has some rather unique features such as a volume slider bar that has no physical button but an area you swipe up and down on.  This works quite well, although it can be adjusted accidentally.  Also a nice feature is the text display which not only helps you to know the device is on but also gives song and audio information.The range of this device is the best that I have seen  and I can go farther away from the bluetooth source than I have previously been able.  The battery also has long life and I have not come into a situation where I ran out of power despite using it all day at work.I never tried out the FM radio features.Overall I am very happy with this bluetooth adapter as it does exactly what I need with no hassles and it allows me to use any headphones I want with it.

First the good:- Battery life - the battery lasts more than 8 hours per charge.  I use this to listen to music at night, and it is still playing the next morning.  I've often forgot to plug in the charger the following morning, but the battery is strong enough to make it through most of the second night.  The battery also does not lose charge during periods of non-usage.  Headset was not used for a week and was left off the charger.  Still had a full battery when I turned it on.- Effortless pairing with phone.  I had to do an initial pairing when I first got it (hold the pairing button for 3 seconds).  Now, when I turn the headset on, it immediately pairs with my phone (Droid Razr Maxx) and beeps to let me know it's paired.- Song readout on the display - displays the current song's ID3 tag.- Earbuds - love the way these fit comfortably into my ears.  They block outside noise very well, and deliver exceptional volume.  I can hear my music just fine over the noise of my lawnmower.- Can pair to multiple devices, so if you have two different bluetooth devices, you can use the same headset.Now the bad:- Volume buttons - you slide your finger across it (towards the headphone jack to increase volume; away from the headphone jack to decrease volume) vice pushing a button.  It may take some getting used to, and I wish they had provided both options so users could either swipe or push the buttons to increase or decrease the volume.- Display readout is upside dowm.  With the shorter earbud in your left ear (as indicated by the L on it), the receiver dangles on your left side.  When you hold it to look at the display (with the headphone jack to the left), the text readout is upside down.  The headphone jack has to lead to the right in order to read the display properly.  If you use your own headphones, this probably won't be an issue, but since I use the ear buds that came with it (with the short cable for the left ear), I'm constantly needing to turn the unit around so I can use the display.- Bright display.  Since I wear these primarily to listen to music while sleeping, I wish they had included a function to lower the display brightness.Other:- I've never used the FM radio function, but it's nice to know it's there in case I need it (e.g., during storms) since the only other FM radio I have is in the car.- The lopsided headphone cord (one long, one short) doesn't seem to bother me.  I simply wrap the long cord around the back of my neck -  which is how I like to wear my headphones while doing yard work, anyway.Overall, an awesome little headset.  For me, the most important factor is battery life, and this one beats all others that I've owned hands down.  I highly recommend this product.

I own an iPad and love to listen to Pandora.  I find that the speaker on the iPad just doesn't cut it at times and I dislike being tethered by wires to my desk while listening at work.  I put a lot of thought and research into a solution that ultimately would make my iPad life a bit better.  I own some pretty high end noise isolating earbuds and prefer using them over anything else while in the office.  This in addition to my want to use the iPad with my home theater (audio only requirement) limited my search to bluetooth receivers with a 3.5mm audio out.I cannot recall exactly, but the other options presented by Amazon (by no easy search!) were a unit by Motorola, an Acoustic Research unit, and some other non-Major manufacturer clip style unit.  Based on the audio quality reviews for the Sony Ericsson model, I chose this product.The product arrived in typical Amazon fashion (fast).  I charged it for the recommended 8+ hour initial charge time and grabbed it on the way out the door to get to the office.  My initial pairing with my iPad was straightforward and without issue.  I'm fairly certain that the iPad has issues pairing with Bluetooth devices with consistent success much like the less than stellar WiFi connectivity that I get.  I did experience a few hiccups trying to get the receiver connected after powering it off and leaving my desk for a while.  Resolution was to turn off bluetooth on the iPad, delete the pairing, and retry.  Since then I've not had issue and iPad Pandora life has been good.  As stated in other reviews, the forward and back controls do not function with Apple products.  When using the receiver, I've also noticed that pressing the Play/Pause button causes my Pandora stream to stop and my iPod iPad app to start playing.  This is slighlty more annoying than not having any function out of the Play/Pause button.My first day of experience with the unit for its office Pandora use has been good.  When connected to my Ultimate Ears SuperFi 5 EB earphones (owned for a few years), I cannot tell the difference between being plugged direct to the iPad or to the bluetooth receiver.  The audio quality offered by Pandora simply doesn't meet audiophile quality recordings (and I'm ok with that).  I have already gotten mostly used to the volume slider reported by others.  It definitely is not perfect.  For my uses, I didn't expect to get song information relayed to the receiver (and it doesn't).  Another note: the volume control on the iPad becomes unavailable when connected to a bluetooth audio receiver.  The bluetooth receiver has sole control of the volume.As I write this review after a full day of work, I see that I've drained only half of the battery level.  I don't listen for the entire day but do when I'm sitting still at my desk.  I'd guess I've listened to about 4 hours of music off and on.I'm interested in seeing how the unit functions at home while connected to speakers in the kitchen, study, and home theater.  I imagine I'll be very pleased with the result.I don't really have plans to pair the unit to my phone but after reading the other reviews, it seems I won't want to replace my already owned Jawbone or BlueAnt headsets.All in all, I give the Sony Ericsson Hi-Fi Bluetooh Stereo Headset a solid 4 stars for use with the Apple iPad.

I brought the Sony Ericsson Hi-Fi Bluetooth Stereo Headset with FM Radio to replace my bluetooth headset,because the battery life was about four hours.Sony ericsson is about eight hours playing music through my phone.To my surprise I left my phone in the basement while talking on it and walked up stairs to the bedroom,I never lost the signal or any sign that I was to far from the phone.Talking in the wind people tell me they notice no deferents in sound quality, very please with my purchase.I would not hesitate to buy again.
Simple function, it works nicely with my MyTouch4g, iPad, and with the FM radio. The sound is good, the transmission distance is fine. The price is good. No complaints at all.
summary: This is really a sweet bluetooth

reviewText: Other reviews have described the unit well, let me share my experiences.I use this device with a Samsung Captivate and an Apple iMac running OSX 10.6 Snow Leopard.It paired with both instantly.On the Captivate, it works as advertised- streams music in surprisingly high fidelity, takes calls (pauses the music), and seems to have built-in background noise suppression (for the mic).  Audio quality listening to music, and on calls is very good.I did an A/B to determine the Bluetooth's effect on sound quality by playing a song on the Captivate through the MW600 for a few seconds, then paused it, swapped the included earbud's jack from the MW600 directly into the Captivate's jack and re-started play.  There was very little sound difference (plugging in directly sounded very slightly better, but not enough to matter).One drawback so far is that the song titles are supposed to display on the MW600's screen, but do not with the Captivate.  This might be an issue with the built-in audio player software in the phone, I'll try some other music software.  As far as I know the Captivate supports all the latest cool-guy Bluetooth standards.One nice plus is that the included charger uses a micro-USB connector, the same as the Captivate (and other phones, I'm sure), so I now have an extra wall charger that will work with both phone and MW600, plus I can use the Captivate's USB to Micro USB charging cable to charge both (off my computer's USB) when I travel and in the car.I paired it with the built-in Bluetooth on my iMac, set it as the audio in/out device in System Preferences> Sound, and played music with iTunes.  The sound quality was very very good, the transport buttons on the MW600 (play/ pause/ FF/ RW) controlled iTunes instantly (no lag), and the song titles DID show up on the MW600, streamed from iTunes, also instantly. Again, the response time from pausing, playing, or skipping forward or back was instantaneous, no lag.  I'm very impressed with the usage of iTunes streamed from the iMac to the MW600, it works perfectly in every way.With Skype, I set the MW600 as the audio in/out in Skype> Preferences, and was a bit buggy at first.  Skype locked up twice when I tried to place a call.  I finally figured out- OSX can see the MW600 as either "Bluetooth Headset" (mono) or "Bluetooth Headphones" (stereo).  If you set it (in System Preferences> Sound) as "Bluetooth Headset" (mono), it works perfectly with Skype.  Skype must not play well with stereo audio over Bluetooth.I placed a Skype test call, recorded my voice and it sounded fine.  Not landline fidelity fine, but o.k. for VoIP.The built in FM radio works well, my only niggle is that you can't program station presets, you either scan through available stations (press and hold to scan to the next strong station) or skip ahead 100KHz at a time (99.1, 99.2, 99.3, etc).  If you're say, at 89 and you want to tune a station at 106, you can't just hold the forward button down and scroll all the way there, you have to go one station at a time, or .1 at a time.  That's a drag.The MW600 automatically displays the station name, ("Jack FM", "KCRW", etc) when you tune it in, then scrolls the artist and song title as it plays (if the station supports it).One final thing, I compared the MW600 ear buds against the ones that came with the Captivate- the Captivate ear buds sound better- more bass, generally higher fidelity, so that supports other comments here that the included ear buds are not the best.  I have a good set of headphones tucked away somewhere, I'm confident that it'll sound great, used for air or train travel, quietly listening in bed at night while reading, etc.Others here have complained about the volume slider.  It is not really an issue for me.  Certainly, it's not as easy to use as a knob, but once you figure it out and use the MW600 a few times, you can get the hang of it.You put your fingertip on the raised slider area, press and slide toward the top of the MW600 (to turn it up).  There's a "+" sign bump at the top, just hold your fingertip there and the volume steadily raises, lift your finger when it's at the volume you want- the display shows a graphic of the volume level.  Do the opposite to lower the volume.  No big deal.So, to summarize, it works perfectly and flawlessly for Bluetooth functions on the iMac- Skype/ VOIP and iTunes streaming.It works nearly perfectly on the Captivate phone, the only minus is that the song titles do not appear in the window.The radio sounds great, has cool display features, but tuning stations is a bit cumbersome.It has a pretty incredible amount of features and quality, stuffed into a very small, very lightweight package.

This blue tooth stereo head set is better than the previous one I had which eventually failed.  There is no discernible bandwidth compression, so sound quality for me is good.  As for complaints, the headphones are light on bass, and there's no tone adjust or bass boost.  I solved the problem by using better headphones, which provide better bass and overall sound.  Also, the volume adjust is electro-static sensing.  If your fingers are dry, it can be tougher to adjust the volume.  And even when your hands aren't dry, it will take one swipe on the volume adjust which calls up the display--the second or third swipe will activate the volume adjust.  I did have one instance when the blue tooth disconnected after setting in standby for more than an hour while watching a movie.  I don't know if that was from the device or the phone, but it never would've happened with a cable stereo headphone connection.  Battery life is good, and still shows full after a full day of use listening to music, though talking on the phone should drain the batteries more quickly.  I would recommend this product based on performance to date.An update to my first review.  I lost the unit, possibly when it caught on my seat belt.  I decided not to buy another one for that reason, though I remain satisfied with its performance.  I've opted for an around the neck unit this time, hoping it will be more difficult to lose.
summary: Works Well, With Just A Few Small Issues

reviewText: This is about the best sounding bluetooth headset that I have.  I can use decent headphones with this and the controls work fairly well. reviewText: I got this one for me and the black one as a gift for my husband. Well, I had a headstart on using this and I have loved it from the beginning. As the other reviewers state, the touch side for the volume is extra sensitive, but I love it. I most definitely recommend this.

**********************************************************BIG NOTE: *** New Addendum***The MW600 has been discontinued (I learned of this on 07/04/12)According to Sony's website, the MW600 is "no longer available." That means that Sony is no longer making the thing nor selling it directly. To replace it, Sony has come up with two things that aren't the positively horrible MW1 (dragged down to a two-stars-out-of-five on Sony's own website... ouch!). The new models will be one without any display and a few control-buttons (which is currently being sold through Amazon) and one, the SBH50, which is basically the MW600 with a larger display, a physical volume control instead of the MW600's electrostatic slider, and an OLED display large enough to read your stream of text messages and caller-ids on--it even maintains the MW600's FM radio. The price-point is as yet unknown (it can only be found on Sony's global website, but intelligent speculation would put it somewhere in the eighty- to one-hundred dollar range. I am looking forward to buying one with my fingers crossed.Why am I crossing my fingers? I haven't seen the SBH50 yet, but if Sony's engineers have done their jobs right, it will be an easier-to-use version of the MW600 with all the kinks worked out ahead of time in the international markets. If they *haven't* done their jobs right, the SBH50 could be another MW1 which all accounts say is a lemon on steroids.The MW600 was an angelic product, (one that actually lists a half-hour battery life improvement on its replacement!) but when the current crop of them is gone, that's all there will ever be of them.I want the new one, but I have no idea how the SBH50 will function and I personally intend to stock up with at least one MW600 before they're gone.For more information on the topic, search for "SBH50" on the web.**********************************************************BIG NOTE: *** New Addendum*** Apple has finally fixed the bluetooth compatability problem in the most current version of MacOs (OSX "Mountain Lion").For the first time, I have had the MW-600 achieve a connection to my iMac and maintain it, in constant or in intermittent use, until the battery on the MW600 runs down. You can now use the MW600 to walk away from your Apple Computer to do the dishes during commercials or get a soft drink and nothing bad will happen.More cause for celebration: the MW600 just bought itself an extra star!***********************************************************This is the full, original review. New notes are in parentheses*The Sony Ericsson MW600s are not perfect, certainly not a panacea, but they function well in multiple roles; offering a stereo bluetooth headset that allows the option of using high-end headphones for improved sound quality and isolation. I voted for them with my own money and, so far, I would be more than happy to buy them again. (I finally destroyed on set after more than year's use--please never ask me how--I bought a new one, in white this time, and I am thinking of buying a second one for dedicated use with my computer for audio and Skype-calls).Before going on to talk about the real, solid reasons for liking them, it is necessary to get other people's reasons for disliking them out of the way. The MW600 has characteristics that some who have reviewed it have called problems. The following things are true about the MW600:1. It is not made of solid titanium.2. It doesn't fit a keyboard's worth of controls onto a two-inch cylinder.3. It offers only partial compatibility with Apple products. (fixed! 08/17/12)4. It is not so simple to set up that a monkey in boxing gloves could do it blindfolded.Now, the good stuff.Physically, the MW600 bluetooth stereo headset is a short, black cylinder with its sides forming a triangle. A clip with a light spring is attached to one angle of it, while the other two angles house controls that let you attach it to devices and control it using a black-and-white, organic light-emitting-diode (OLED) display.Its overall length without headphones is shorter than my pinky and yet it interfaces with many bluetooth-equipped computers, smartphones, and music/movie players with limited compatibility with Apple's iPod Touch and iPad (this has since been improved in later versions of iOS and OSX Mountain Lion. 08/17/12)Unlike it's predecessors, the MW600 has a headphone jack instead of fixed headphones meaning that it can accept any stereo headphones with a standard 3.5mm plug. The headphones that come with it have a short cord and offer very good reproduction for the sort of sound that comes from a portable player, but the fact that you can plug anything you like into them offers you the option of swapping out the units that come with it for better headphones, including audiophile-level units (high-impedence units like Grado SR-60s will work with the MW600, but it doesn't have the oomph to get the best from them, nearly all buds are okay and some are surprising. 08/17/12).For people who need better sound or louder volume this is a definite cause for celebration.  It means convenience: it means that users with high-quality, two-part headphones of the kind made by companies like Shure and Denon can integrate them into their telephones via bluetooth for enhanced call-quality; it means that exercise-lovers can use high-end equipment while running on treadmills and it means that someone sitting in a cafe can stand up and stretch without having to disassemble their set-up first.Call quality on the user's end with the MW600 is as good as you can expect when the sound of the caller's voice is sent directly to both the receiver's ears while MW600's microphone seems adequately sensitive and wind-resistant.Of course, nothing is perfect and the MW600 is no exception. The MW600 is not for people who can't be bothered to learn control sequences of simian complexity, or who are too sensitive to put up with the limitations of an interface that runs off of four buttons and a (slightly frustrating) volume slider to control a device that is smaller than the average matchbox.Also, Sony and Apple are not the best of friends and the Sony device's music controls aren't recognized by Apple devices, including computers (this has changed, the MW600 will now connect reliably to an iMac running OSX Mountain Lion 08/17/12). The MW600 will interface with and play output from Apple devices, but the controls on the MW600 only play/pause the iPod Touch/iPad. They will not fast-forward, select, skip or do anything else to the actual music sequence.This means the user of any of Apple's i-devices will have to undergo the ultimate hardship to change tracks or playlists: he will have to reach into his pocket and use the iPod's physical controls, supporting the brutishly heavy machine in his hand for second, after grueling second...At the end of the day, it is hard to call the MW600 a bluetooth device because it goes above and beyond the great majority of bluetooth devices, offering a power and flexibility that makes it better than nearly everything out there, including stereo units like the Motorola Motorokr M9s and single-ear bluetooth units like the various Jawbone devices that can cost nearly twice as much. Even paired with good headphones, their sound is never as good as a metal-to-metal connection's is, but with good headphones, for bluetooth, they're a revelation.Oh, I almost forgot: they threw in an FM radio for free.(addendum 08/15/2010: After several hours of listening to an audiobook on my iPod Touch at work, the iPod touch ran out of power (in part because of the high power demands of using bluetooth). I set it on a charger a substantial distance from where I was standing and I found that I could still keep listening to it using the MW600 with no loss of sound quality. The pause/play function worked fine with me standing where I was with a closed door between myself and my player.)(addendum 09/01/2010: Trying to use this device, sharing it between multiple Apple devices, can cause frustrating connection problems. After connecting it to my computer, iPod Touch and iPad, I soon found it necessary to erase profiles and start over from scratch when connecting. Other companies make bluetooth gear that handles this more easily. Also, the general incompatibility of Sony and Apple bluetooth hardware (mentioned above) can cause problems on the computer side when you attempt multiple pairings with devices of the same type (largely fixed, as of 08/17/12).I still like the things (I've used them to listen to an audiobook playing on an ipod that was charging 30 feet away), but I have to say that I like them less (they're much improved in value by the enhanced Apple-compatability 08/17/12)
summary: Not Perfect but Some Cause for Celebration (more cause as of 08/17/12... See Below

I had bought this item on ebay on 10/05/2010 and after it arrived I've been wearing it almost every day since. It is a very good bluetooth headset, sound quality is great (to an average music consumer, not audiophile level of course) and you can literally leave your cellphone a couple of feet away (or put it inside your backpack for that matter) and the headset would still receive the signal crystal clear. I didn't measure it but it must've been about 7 to 8 meters or more without any wall in between and about the half of that in between rooms (let's say you left your cellphone on your bedroom and went to the bathroom with the headset on, in my case it barely made it). The thing is that with the regular use you will not suffer from missing BT signal issues.When the device is new battery life is about 8 hours which is perfect for my daily commute (about ~66 minutes of music listening each day: ~33 minutes of going to work, and ~33 coming back). If you plan on using this device to listen to music for long periods you may have to charge it almost daily or every two days. Which would suck because it does take a while, almost three hours so take this into account. Since I use other headphones at work this wasn't an issue for me. When it has about 30mins worth of energy left it will warn you with a little sound which is nice.After a year of use the battery starts to drain faster, which is to be expected. I got one hour and a half less after a year. The same happened after the second year but I didn't measure it accurately. And about two months ago sometimes I just got two hours off of it, and sometimes the battery would just die after an hour and a half with no warning. When it died on me I just connected the headphones directly to my cellphone, which I had to put on the pocket of my shirt.The headset it's been wearing down for a while now. The clip was the first thing to go, it broke down after about 1.5 years, luckily I could find it (since it fell to the ground before I realized that it wasn't there. I use this clip under my shirt) and I arranged a rubber band around it so it would still "clip". To me, the clip is why this device doesn't get the full four stars, it's very low quality and it is a fundamental part of this headset, Sony can make a better clip than this. And the headphone broke about the same day that arrived this new unit (8/21/2013) which was a relieve.The cord of the right headphone is a little bit shorter on this new unit, which is nice because it was too long on the original and I had to work around it to make it shorter.I bought another unit because this model is designed in a way that is just so convenient to me, much more than all the other BT headphones around (there has been incredibly slow progress on the BT headphones front). It is very non intrusive. The battery life is good for my use, the same for it's quality, my main issue really is the clip. Listen up Sony!

It doesn't always respond when you want it to, and it gets in the way when you are just trying to hold the device. It can actually get rather frustrating. Also, since the device selection (switching from phone to pc, etc) relies on the volume control, it doesn't work as well as it should either.This next problem is probably on my end, but I thought i'd mention it. I like that I can use my own headphones, though it does add bulk for sure. Also, FM reception is good. reviewText: I've owned two now. The first stopped powering on after a few weeks,  but I loved it so much that I returned the first and ordered a second unit. A quick search of the internet will show that many users have experienced the same power issues, so I knew I may have this issue the second time around. So far so good however! What I love about this device:Battery lifeTruly epic.  I listen to either bluetooth or the on board fm tuner all day (when starting from a full charge)  without so much as a worry. It just keeps going and going and going......... You get the picture!FM TunerThis is invaluable to those of us with limited data plans who can't afford to be streaming all day long. Although I am not one of those few (my data plan is unlimited), I still listen to the fm tuner when I feel the need for a change. Like many other cell phone or mobile devices,  your headphone is the antenna so you cannot really blame reception issues on the MW600. That said,  reception is very reliable and strong and in my metro (Orlando)  I can usually listen to the radio all day along without issue.Feature setI can do something on this device that I cannot do on many other bluetooth devices. I can split profiles. On my work phone (a bonafide dumbphone)  ii usually connect the phone profile,  and on my personal phone,  a tmo gsii,  I connect the media profile. I hadn't been able to do this prior with any other bluetooth device, so this was a pleasant surprise.  This split profile management can be controlled directly from the MW600 because of the lcd screen, and indeed it operates flawlessly.LCD ScreenHighly useful and very visible even in daylight. It features a simple black background with white text & icons, so contrast is no issue. The iconography is very clear from identifying which particular phone you're connecting to,  to volume level display etc. Its much better than the audio cues that most other devices rely on.Audio qualityI immediately replaced the supplied buds with a Samsung set. There was no low frequency reproduction,  mids were ok and the highs were somewhat lacking. The Samsungs were much better in all these areas.  Even so,  the beauty of the MW600 is that you can plug in whatever high quality headset that suits you best because it features a 3.5mm headset on top which allows that. So kudos to Sony for including that.OverallTheres a reason I bought two,  and its because its worth it. If my second unit craps out and Amazon takes it back I dont see a reason not to buy a third.  There's probably nothing that tops it in features on the market at this point in time.  Sony should work on the long term  quality though,  then this would indeed be a 5 star product. Til then 4 stars very well describes the quality and worth of this product.
I got it as per the description and i'm happy with the product. Its worth for the money you pay. Thanks

I'm pretty well impressed with this headset, as it does all its intended functions, and mostly does them well. Calls and music are both very clear, and it's nice to have fully functional remote control buttons for the music attached to my collar.The one thing I'm not a fan of is the volume control. I wish there was just a pushbutton rather than the slide sensor. I see why they chose the sensor over a button since there are buttons on the opposite side that have different functions and simply squeezing the device to turn up the volume might inadvertently just change tracks instead. You can also use the slider (after long pressing the talk button) to change between paired devices. Unfortunately, for both volume control and device switching, the sensor isn't very, well, sensitive. I have to try over and over and over again to get it to do what I want. Maybe my skin's too dry?  I have no idea.Currently, I have this thing paired with both my personal and work phones, as well as my iPod. It's only supposed to support two devices, but I made it work so that it's connected to both my iPod and phone at the same time. Basically, the phonecall-handling side of the headset and the music-handling side of the headset are, in a way, separate devices. I paired the iPod to both "device slots" first, and then paired my personal phone to slot 1 and my work phone to slot 2. Now, whichever phone I'm connected to, the music-handling side is already connected to the iPod. This lets me listen to music while I work, and then switch over to phonecalls as needed. It isn't flawless, and I don't expect it to be since it probably wasn't designed for this. If the phone starts ringing while I'm listening to music, I can no longer pause the music by hitting the play button. I can answer the call by hitting the talk button, and this effectively pauses the music, but more because it disconnects from the iPod than anything else. When the phonecall is over, I can hit the play button and the headset will try its best to reconnect to the iPod and resume playing. Sometimes it takes a little more coaxing via rebooting the headset or fiddling with the iPod bluetooth connection settings.Another interesting thing I've noticed is that if I've got this headset connected to my iPod and plug my car's aux-in cable into the headphone jack, music will come over the car stereo but I can still control play/pause/skip via the headset. Neat! It's like an iPod remote control. Oh, and since this thing has a standard 3.5mm headphone jack, I can also unplug the earbuds and just plug the aux-in cable into the headset and it works great that way too. This also works on my home stereo. I tried using this setup as a speakerphone and had mixed results. Not surprised, as it's not meant for this use. Your mileage may vary.This headset works best with a shirt with a collar, like a polo or button-up shirt. You can wear it with t-shirts, but it's really not meant for it. The end of the thing always ends up poking into my neck the whole time and I can't figure a way to position it that isn't annoying or uncomfortable. The text display is "neat" but good luck reading it without removing it from your shirt.All in all, this thing is a great device and if the volume control wasn't so frustrating would definitely be a 5-star product.
summary: Pretty good, but could be a bit better.

reviewText: This is my second Bluetooth pair of headphones, having come from the Motorola s305's. The s305's are good, but these Sony MW600's offer a lot more features, and a design that may be more appealing to some. Unfortunately, the design has a few problems that undermine an otherwise brilliant device.First let me say that as far as function is concerned, I couldn't be happier with the MW600's. I love the fact that I can pair the unit with three different devices and easily switch between them. I have set it up to work with my PC for Skyping, and my iphone for phone calls and music as well. Though I don't have a PS3 yet, I plan on getting one and using the MW600 so that I can play games and watch movies without disturbing others in the house. The reception and range on the MW600's are also impressive. They easily meet the stated range of 30 feet without dropping at all,though thick walls do limit that range somewhat. That range means that I can easily do skype calls with my PC in my home office while I wander around my house doing other things. And when I'm in the office, I like to listen to music (and blot out the office noise) without being tied in to my machine - I am free to roam and get a cup of coffee without taking off my headphones. The stereo sound is good for music as well, though I suspect that a slightly nicer pair of earbuds would improve it, and I plan on getting a nicer pair to test that theory. The MW600's design allows for that, and also allows the unit to be plugged into other stereo systems, including car stereo systems, which I have done. It's very handy to be able to play music from my iPhone without needing to actually jack it in to the car - so handy, actually, that I'm thinking of getting a second MW600 just for car use. As someone who goes to the gym and runs outside on a regular basis, I like being able to use the MW600 both with my iPhone (in my pocket or resting on the running machine) or just on it's own to listen to the radio as well, I wish the unit allowed for presets, but since I pretty much just listen to two different stations it's not that big a deal. I love the fact that the unit allows for voice activated calling as well (when paired with a compatible phone) and that incoming phone numbers with caller ID are displayed on the units LCD screen. In short, this is a great device for home, home office, office, car and gym.Now to the problems; the size of the MW600 is pretty small - about the size of a AA battery. The problem is that the buttons that control the functions cover almost every surface of the unit, making it hard to touch the device without triggering some function. Of particular frustration is the volume button, which covers the entire left side of the unit. Not only does touching it sometimes trigger the volume control, but it is not always responsive when you actually intend to change the volume. Because the ff, rw and play buttons cover the right side, it's very easy to accidentally skip ahead; annoying when listening to music but utterly enraging when listening to a podcast, for instance. It would make sense then, when readjusting the device, to grab it gingerly by the top, but of course this is where the "phone" button is located, which triggers voice activated commands on many phones. So while it is great that there are so many features in this tiny package, it can be frustrating to access (or not access) them.Other little things that I like; micro-USB charging and long battery life, LED displays radio station ID and caller ID, alligator clip holds well and clips nicely to button down shirts and coats. Other little things that I don't like: included earphones are a little too short, LED doesn't display song ID, really needs a lanyard to be used for workouts (i.e t-shirts) and it would be nice to be able to remove the alligator clip in that instanceI like these headphones well enough to keep them and I'm hoping at over time my frustrations will fade a bit, but I'm looking forward to the next version that keeps all the features but makes the headphones easier to use.
summary: The best, and the worst, of Bluetooth headphones
